title: An mRNA–lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 influenza virus protects lactating dairy cows from infection - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus has recently emerged in dairy cattle in the USA, leading to mastitis and sharp reductions in milk production. The main site of H5N1 viral replication is the mammary tissue rather than the respiratory tract and viral transmission between animals is thought to occur through viral shedding in milk. Here, we generate an mRNA–lipid nanoparticle (mRNA–LNP) vaccine encoding the hemagglutinin (HA) of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, representative of circulating bovine H5N1 viruses, and assess its immunogenicity and efficacy in lactating dairy cows. Eight cows were divided into vaccinated and control groups, receiving two intramuscular doses of the vaccine or saline, followed by intramammary viral challenge. Vaccination elicited HA-reactive and neutralizing antibodies in serum and HA-reactive antibodies in milk. Following viral challenge, vaccinated cows had ~1,000-fold lower peak viral RNA in milk and a lower occurrence of mastitis and mammary fibrosis.

MainHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus continues to cause widespread outbreaks among wild birds and mammals in North America, as well as on commercial poultry farms. In 2024, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b emerged in cattle in the USA and quickly spread to animals in 19 states1. The H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b outbreak in cattle has already caused major economic losses in the dairy industry2 and represents a concern for human health because of the increased risk of mammalian adaptation and potential human-to-human transmission3.H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus causes limited respiratory signs in cattle. While the virus can be sporadically detected from oronasally inoculated calves under experimental conditions4,5,6, the respiratory tract is not likely the primary site of viral replication. Instead, the main site of H5N1 viral replication is the mammary tissue of infected lactating animals. Experimental intramammary inoculation with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses leads to reduced feed intake and rumen motility, as well as drastic reductions in milk production because of severe mastitis4,5,7,8. H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses exhibit tropism for the mammary gland tissue of cows9,10, as confirmed by the presence of viral RNA and antigen in the alveolar milk-secreting epithelial cells and the interlobular space of infected animals8. Additionally, mastitis caused by the H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus affects the color and consistency of milk and changes in the mammary tissue contribute to the dramatic reduction in milk production4.In addition to enhanced biosecurity efforts, the use of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 vaccines in cattle has been considered11. Vaccination can potentially aid in controlling the current outbreak in lactating dairy cows, limiting the drop in milk production in exposed animals and reducing the risk of spillover events into humans. Some bovine vaccines elicit antibodies that are transferred into milk in lactating animals. For example, the Mycobacterium bovis-BoHV-1 combined vaccine effectively elicits antigen-specific maternal antibodies12 and an inactivated H5 avian influenza A virus vaccine elicits antibodies in both serum and milk13. While other vaccines against the HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus have been tested in bovine animal models6,13,14,15,16, studies are needed to systematically evaluate the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of vaccines in lactating dairy cows against intramammary infection, as the mammary glands are the site for HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus infection4,5.We previously developed an mRNA–LNP vaccine encoding an HA from a clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus and demonstrated that the vaccine elicited robust immune responses in mice and ferrets, preventing morbidity and mortality in ferrets following HPAI 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus challenge17. We found that the same mRNA–LNP vaccine was immunogenic in calves, inducing a strong antibody and T cell-mediated immune response that reduces viral shedding from experimental HPAI 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus infection6. In the present study, we evaluated the immunogenicity and efficacy of a clade 2.3.4.4b H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine administered to lactating dairy cows. We found that the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine elicited strong antibody responses in both serum and milk. Additionally, the vaccine significantly reduced virus replication and disease, including clinical mastitis, associated with clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 intramammary route of infection.ResultsH5 mRNA–LNP vaccines are well tolerated in lactating dairy cattleWe generated an mRNA vaccine that expresses the hemagglutinin (HA) of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, which is representative of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses currently circulating in dairy cattle in the USA4. We vaccinated four lactating dairy cows intramuscularly with 500 μg of H5 mRNA–LNP in saline and then boosted intramuscularly with the same vaccine dose 3 weeks later (Fig. 1a). As a control, we intramuscularly injected four additional lactating cows twice with saline (Fig. 1a). Animals in our study were obtained from an HPAI-monitored Holstein dairy herd in Pennsylvania and ranged from 2 to 8 years of age (Supplementary Table 1). We collected serum samples at 0, 7, 21, 28, 41 and 49 days after the initial vaccination and collected milk samples daily. Both unvaccinated and vaccinated animals were challenged with infectious clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus through intramammary inoculation 49 days after the first vaccination.Fig. 1: Vaccination study design, safety and mRNA–LNP vaccine immunogenicity in lactating dairy cows.Full size imagea, Overview of the vaccination and sampling scheme. Lactating dairy cows were vaccinated using a prime-boost regimen. Milk and blood samples were collected at different time points. At 49 days after vaccination and 28 days after boost, lactating dairy cows were challenged with HPAIV H5N1 and monitored daily for signs of disease and virus shedding. i.m.m., intramammary. Data shown are the mean of two replicates. d, H5-specific IgG antibody levels were measured by ELISA in sera from unvaccinated (open red triangles) and vaccinated (closed black circles) animals and endpoint titers are shown. e, Neutralizing antibodies were measured using a 90% FRNT; the reciprocal dilutions of serum required to inhibit 90% of virus infection are shown. f,g, HAI antibodies were measured by HAI assay in sera at 49 (f) and 63 (g) days after vaccination; reciprocal dilutions of serum required to prevent red blood cell agglutination are shown. h, H5-specific IgG antibody levels were measured by ELISA in milk and endpoint titers are shown. Data are the mean ± s.e.m. and individual data points (n = 4) are shown. Dashed lines indicate the lower limit of detection. Significant statistical differences (P < 0.05) between groups were determined using a log-normal two-tailed t-test with Welch correction and are indicated by an asterisk.Source dataThe vaccine was well tolerated, with no obvious adverse effects. Previous studies found trace amounts of vaccine-related mRNA in human milk in some individuals shortly after SARS-CoV-2 mRNA–LNP vaccination18,19,20. Therefore, we completed experiments to determine whether we could detect H5 mRNA–LNP in bovine milk samples obtained after vaccination. First, we established a sensitive quantitative PCR assay to measure H5 mRNA levels in milk. We spiked a milk sample from an unvaccinated cow with a known concentration of the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine to assess the sensitivity of our PCR assay (Extended Data Fig. 1). We found that the detection limit of our assay was 65 mRNA copies per μl. We then used quantitative PCR (qPCR) to measure H5 mRNA levels in milk samples collected up to 8 days after prime or boost vaccination. None of the milk samples from vaccinated animals had detectable levels of H5 mRNA (Fig. 1b,c), demonstrating that vaccine-derived mRNA was not present at detectable levels in milk after intramuscular vaccination of lactating dairy cows.H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine is immunogenic in lactating dairy cattleWe quantified the level of H5-reactive antibodies in the sera from vaccinated animals and performed functional assays to determine whether these antibodies could inhibit H5N1 virus infection. We detected low levels of H5-reactive IgG in sera as early as 21 days after vaccination that significantly increased after booster vaccination (Fig. 1d). Unexpectedly, we found that one cow from the unvaccinated group and one cow from the vaccinated group had low levels of H5-reactive serum IgG before the start of the experiment but were below the limit of detection in the H5 neutralizing assay (day 0; Fig. 1d,e). The source herd was under weekly HPAI surveillance before and during the study and remained HPAI negative, suggesting that the low levels of H5-reactive IgG in these animals was not because of H5N1 infection. A recent study reported that 2.6% of cattle in the USA have serological evidence of past exposures to human influenza A virus21; therefore, we hypothesized that the low levels of H5-reactive IgG in two of the animals in our study were because of cross-reactive antibodies elicited by human influenza virus infections. Consistent with this idea, the two animals that had low but detectable H5 IgG antibodies before the study also had detectable H1-reactive antibodies (Extended Data Fig. 2). All four vaccinated animals, including the one animal with low levels of preexisting antibodies, produced similar levels of H5 antibodies following vaccination (Fig. 1d,e).We completed in vitro neutralization assays to determine whether serum antibodies could prevent infection of the A/dairy cattle/Texas/2024 H5N1 virus. Consistent with the IgG binding data, H5N1 neutralizing antibodies were detected as early as 21 days after vaccination and were significantly increased after booster vaccination (Fig. 1e). We also completed hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) assays using sera collected just before viral challenge to determine whether vaccine-elicited antibodies blocked viral attachment. Consistent with both the IgG binding and in vitro neutralization data, we found that antibodies in the sera from all four vaccinated animals blocked viral attachment to erythrocytes (Fig. 1f). Vaccine-elicited antibodies were boosted after H5N1 challenge, rising to levels observed in unvaccinated challenged animals (Fig. 1g).We also quantified H5-reactive IgG levels in milk samples collected in our study. H5-reactive IgG was detected in only one vaccinated cow after the first vaccination (in one of the vaccinated animals without preexisting antibody) (Fig. 1h). We detected high levels of H5-reactive IgG in milk from all four vaccinated animals following the booster vaccination (Fig. 1h). Peak levels of H5-reactive IgG were higher in sera compared to milk and antibody levels declined more rapidly in milk compared to the sera (Extended Data Fig. 3). We were unable to perform in vitro neutralization with milk samples as nonspecific inhibitors in milk from unvaccinated animals inhibit virus in these assays.Specificity of antibodies elicited by H5 mRNA–LNP vaccinationWe performed pseudovirus deep mutational scanning experiments22 to identify HA epitopes targeted by neutralizing antibodies in sera from lactating dairy cows vaccinated with the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine (Fig. 2). For these experiments, we incubated bovine sera with a pool of nonreplicative lentiviral particles that were pseudotyped with mutant HAs from the clade 2.3.4.4b A/American Wigeon/South Carolina/USDA-000345-001/2021 virus, as previously described23. This H5 deep mutational scanning library carries nearly all of the 10,773 possible amino acid substitutions in the HA23. We found that the neutralizing activity of the sera from all four vaccinated animals targeted the antigenic sites on the globular head of HA (Fig. 2a,b), including antigenic site A (residues 124–127 and 144–145, H3 numbering) and antigenic site B (residues 165, 167, 169 and 171, H3 numbering). There was a remarkable similarity in the amino acid sites targeted by the serum antibodies isolated from individual vaccinated cows. These data indicate that most neutralizing antibodies elicited by the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine target neutralizing epitopes adjacent to the receptor-binding domain of HA. Importantly, the amino acid identities at the sites most strongly targeted by the vaccine-induced neutralizing antibodies are not highly variable in the HA of circulating clade 2.3.4.4b viruses (Fig. 2c).Fig. 2: Effect of substitutions in HA on vaccinated cattle sera neutralization.Full size imagea, Neutralization decrease caused by substitutions at each position in HA. The top plot shows the mean total neutralization decrease for the four vaccinated cow sera and the plots below show the individual cow neutralization decrease. Sites causing the greatest neutralization decrease are labeled by amino acid position above the top plot. b, Mean effects of substitutions at each site of cattle serum neutralization overlaid on a surface representation of HA (Protein Data Bank (PDB) accession 4KWM). Sites are colored white if substitutions have no effect on neutralization and red if substitutions decrease neutralization. c, Amino acid conservation at HA sites where substitutions caused the greatest neutralization decrease by the vaccinated cow sera, calculated over all available H5 sequences, 2.3.4.4b clade sequences and B3.13 and D1.1 genotype sequences from dairy cows.Source dataH5 mRNA–LNP vaccination protects lactating cows from H5N1 infectionTo determine whether H5 mRNA–LNP vaccination can prevent virus shedding and reduce H5N1 disease, we experimentally challenged unvaccinated and vaccinated cows with clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024) through the intramammary inoculation route and monitored the cows for 14 days after inoculation. We then humanely euthanized the animals and performed macroscopic and microscopic lesion analyses.We measured levels of H5N1 viral RNA in milk samples by quantitatice reverse transcription PCR (RT–qPCR) assays. In unvaccinated animals, H5N1 viral RNA in milk from inoculated mammary quarters was first detected at 1 day after inoculation and peaked at 2 days after inoculation; milk samples remained RT–qPCR-positive throughout the study period (Fig. 3a). In vaccinated animals, H5N1 viral RNA levels in milk from inoculated mammary quarters were significantly lower at 1–3, 5 and 8–13 days after inoculation, with ~1,000-fold lower peak titer compared to levels found in milk from unvaccinated animals (Fig. 3a). Most milk samples that were positive for H5N1 viral RNA by RT–qPCR with cycle threshold (Ct) < 35 contained infectious H5N1 virus (Supplementary Table 2). We detected either H5N1 viral RNA or infectious virus in milk from the uninoculated quarters of two unvaccinated animals (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 2), suggesting that virus was able to migrate from an inoculated to uninoculated quarter in these animals. We detected viral antigen in mammary tissue from uninoculated quarters of both unvaccinated and vaccinated animals using immunohistochemistry (IHC) (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5a,b); however, viral RNA in the milk from uninoculated mammary quarters in vaccinated animals was below the limit of detection, suggesting that the vaccine prevented further spread of the virus.Fig. 3: Virus RNA detection in clinical samples from unvaccinated and vaccinated lactating cows after challenge.Full size imagea, The log10-transformed TCID50 per ml equivalent Ct detection of virus RNA in stripped milk from inoculated mammary quarters of unvaccinated (open red triangles) and vaccinated (closed black circles) lactating dairy cows. Data shown are the mean ± s.e.m. of n = 4. Significant statistical differences (P < 0.05) between groups were determined using a mixed-effects model (residual maximum likelihood model) followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparison test. Time points with a significant difference (P < 0.05) between unvaccinated and vaccinated are indicated by an asterisk. b, qPCR quantification of virus RNA from antemortem clinical samples of unvaccinated and vaccinated lactating dairy cows. A Ct below 35 was considered positive (red), a Ct between 35 and 38 was considered suspect (yellow) and a Ct above 38 was considered negative (white). LL, LeucoLOCK from whole blood; NA, not applicable; NS, nasal swab; OS, ocular swab.Source dataWe measured H5N1 RNA levels in other clinical samples, including nasal swabs, ocular swabs, urine, saliva, serum and whole blood. We detected H5 RNA in multiple sample types from all four unvaccinated animals (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4). By contrast, few samples obtained from vaccinated animals possessed detectable levels of H5 RNA (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4). We also collected fresh mammary tissue, supramammary lymph nodes and a section of diaphragm at the necropsy 14 days after inoculation. H5 RNA was detected in mammary tissue from inoculated quarters in all unvaccinated cows, in an uninoculated quarter of one unvaccinated cow and only in inoculated quarters of two vaccinated cows, as well as in an uninoculated quarter of one vaccinated animal using IHC (Extended Data Fig. 4). Supramammary lymph node tissue was positive for H5 RNA in three unvaccinated cows and in two vaccinated cows and diaphragm liquid was suspect in one unvaccinated cow (Extended Data Fig. 4).Following H5N1 virus infection, unvaccinated cows displayed decreased rumen motility 1–7 days after inoculation, with a significant decrease at 3 and 4 days after inoculation (Fig. 4a). Milk production also significantly decreased in unvaccinated animals following H5N1 infection, beginning at 2 days after inoculation, with a dramatic drop at 3 days after inoculation that remained significantly reduced throughout the study at 4–8 and 10–12 days after inoculation (Fig. 4b). Rumen motility and milk production were less impacted in vaccinated cows following H5N1 infection (Fig. 4a,b). We observed severe changes in color (Fig. 4c) and consistency (Fig. 4d) indicative of mastitis in milk from the inoculated mammary quarters of unvaccinated cows following H5N1 infection. By contrast, milk color and consistency from inoculated mammary quarters of vaccinated cows were less affected by H5N1 infection (Fig. 4c,d). Uninoculated mammary quarters of unvaccinated cows also displayed changes in milk color and consistency, albeit to a lesser extent compared to inoculated mammary quarters (Fig. 4c,d). Furthermore, unvaccinated cows showed signs of mastitis in inoculated quarters and, to a lesser extent, in uninoculated quarters, as determined by California mastitis test (CMT) (Fig. 4e). Inoculated quarters from unvaccinated animals consistently scored above 2 (score range: 0–3) in the CMT, which indicates moderate to severe inflammation and leukocyte infiltration. Conversely, inoculated and uninoculated mammary quarters of vaccinated cows frequently scored a CMT below 1 following H5N1 virus infection (Fig. 4e), indicating little to no signs of mastitis. The clinical mastitis scores in uninoculated quarters were primarily contributed by two unvaccinated cows (Fig. 4c–e). We found that unvaccinated cows had a significant association between loss in milk production, clinical signs, and viral RNA detections in milk of inoculated quarters. By contrast, vaccinated cows did not present a significant association among loss in milk production, clinical signs and viral RNA in milk, except for rumination time (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). Data shown are the mean of n = 4 per treatment group.Source dataH5 mRNA–LNP vaccination of lactating cows significantly decreased mammary fibrosisWe completed macroscopic evaluation of the mammary glands from inoculated and uninoculated quarters for all lactating dairy cows at necropsy. Consistent with the clinical observations, inoculated mammary quarters from unvaccinated cows exhibited significantly higher macroscopic lesion scores compared to vaccinated cows (P < 0.05; 95.4 and 8.1; Fig. 5a). By contrast, macroscopic lesion scores in uninoculated mammary quarters were low and did not differ significantly between unvaccinated and vaccinated cows (P > 0.05; 12.1 to 10.0; Supplementary Table 3). A representative image of normal mammary tissue in an uninoculated quarter is shown in Fig. 5b and an image of fibrotic mammary tissue in an inoculated quarter of an unvaccinated cow is shown in Fig. 5c. Consistent with the macroscopic scores, microscopic scores of mammary gland fibrosis using Picrosirius red staining demonstrated less fibrosis in inoculated glands from vaccinated animals compared to unvaccinated animals (Fig. 5d–h and Supplementary Tables 4 and 7). A histologically unremarkable photomicrograph of mammary tissue is shown in Fig. 5e for comparison and representative photomicrographs are shown with tissue from a vaccinated uninoculated cow (Fig. 5f), a vaccinated inoculated cow (Fig. 5g) and an unvaccinated inoculated cow (Fig. 5h).Fig. 5: Macroscopic and microscopic lesions in mammary tissue after challenge.Full size imagea, The percentages of macroscopic lesions in the mammary tissue of unvaccinated and vaccinated lactating dairy cows were measured in inoculated quarters. Data shown are the calculated average percentage (0–100) of the rostral, mid and caudal regions for inoculated quarters (mean ± s.e.m. of n = 4). b, Macroscopic photo representative of a normal mammary tissue producing milk (cow 2, unvaccinated rear right uninoculated quarter). c, Representative photo of mastitis-affected mammary tissue with fibrosis (cow 2, rear left inoculated quarter). d, The percentage of microscopic lesions in the mammary tissue of unvaccinated and vaccinated lactating dairy cows. Data shown are the calculated median score of the rostral, mid and caudal regions for inoculated quarters (scale 0–144; n = 4). e, Picrosirius red stain of mammary gland highlighting connective tissue and fibrosis (red). A histologically unremarkable photomicrograph was included for comparative purposes. Thin bands of supporting connective tissue (arrowhead) separate lobules and no to minimal intralobular collagen (cow 6, front left quarter, vaccinated, uninoculated, fibrosis score = 0). Representative photomicrographs were selected on the basis of their alignment with the mean fibrosis score for the respective group. f, Extensive interlobular fibrosis with lobular separation (arrowhead) and dense intralobular collagen (arrow) with partial lobular disruption (cow 5, front left quarter, vaccinated uninoculated, fibrosis score = 9). g, Thick interlobular collagen bundles with compression of adjacent lobules (arrowhead) and increased intralobular collagen (arrow) with mild distortion of lobular architecture (cow 7, front right quarter, vaccinated inoculated, fibrosis score = 9). h, Extensive interlobular fibrosis with lobular separation (arrowhead) and dense intralobular collagen (arrow) with near complete lobular disruption (cow 4, rear left quarter, unvaccinated inoculated, fibrosis score = 14).DiscussionThe recent widespread outbreaks of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b virus in dairy cattle, along with its association with milk loss and severe mastitis, require effective countermeasures for the dairy industry. In one study, decreased milk production, mortality and early herd removal of lactating cows clinically affected by HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b virus resulted in economic losses of 950 USD per clinically affected cow, totaling approximately 737,500 USD for the infected herd that was studied2. Vaccines that reduce clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus in milk might be useful in preventing the spread of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses in lactating cattle. Combined with robust viral testing programs, a 2.3.4.4b H5N1 vaccine has the potential to reduce virus transmission, clinical signs and mastitis in H5N1-infected lactating dairy cattle, while limiting potential viral spillovers into humans and other susceptible wild and domestic animal populations.Recent studies have evaluated the immunogenicity of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 inactivated13,16, DNA-based16 and mRNA–LNP15 vaccines in lactating dairy cows. These studies have demonstrated that different vaccine platforms are capable of eliciting H5-reactive antibodies in cows but more in-depth comparative challenge studies are needed to evaluate how different vaccine platforms affect milk production, rumination and virus-induced mastitis. Our study provides a comprehensive and quantitative assessment of an H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine against intramammary HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus infection in lactating dairy cows. We found that our H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine induced neutralizing antibodies in lactating dairy cows and protected against intramammary HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus infection. We found that rumination and milk production dropped more in unvaccinated cows relative to vaccinated cows following H5N1 infection. The vaccine was well tolerated and animals showed no apparent adverse events following vaccination. We did not detect H5 mRNA in milk collected after intramuscular vaccine administration, supporting its safety for cows and their milk. Furthermore, the H5 mRNA–LNP reduced peak H5N1 viral titers in milk ~1,000-fold. While it is reasonable to suspect that this large reduction in viral titers will limit animal-to-animal H5N1 transmission, additional large-scale field experiments will be required to test this possibility. Previous studies have demonstrated that intramuscular immunization of HA mRNA–LNP or conventional influenza vaccines can reduce influenza virus transmission in ferrets, pigs and guinea pigs24,25,26,27 and future experiments should evaluate whether our H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine reduces H5N1 transmission in lactating dairy cows.The H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine elicited antibody responses in both serum and milk. Antibody levels in milk were consistently lower compared to those in serum before challenge. This was expected, considering the varying concentrations of IgG present in milk after the periparturient and colostrogenesis periods. Future studies are needed to investigate the impact of different routes of immunization, vaccination schedules and vaccine doses on the magnitude and longevity of antibody responses elicited by mRNA–LNP vaccines in cattle. It is critical to continue optimizing vaccine regimens that elicit sustained protective levels of antibodies in the milk of lactating cattle, with the goal of optimizing a vaccine that elicits protective antibody titers after a single immunization. Additionally, it will be important to consider a differentiating infected from vaccinated animals (DIVA) strategy for diagnostics and HPAI outbreak investigation in vaccinated livestock. As our H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine elicited only antibody responses to the HA protein, the detection of NP antibodies would indicate a natural infection and could be used as a DIVA strategy.HPAI H5N1 2.3.4.4b has a high tropism for the mammary gland and infects milk-secreting mammary epithelial cells lining the alveoli, resulting in a viral-induced mastitis8. Experimental inoculation of lactating cows with HPAI H5 2.3.4.4b through the intramammary route recapitulates field observations, leading to severe acute mammary gland infections with necrotizing mastitis5. In affected mammary tissue, 15–50% of the secretory alveoli and ducts, both intralobular and interlobular, are replaced by fibrous connective tissue4. In our studies, we used a special collagen stain to directly compare fibrosis in mammary tissue caused by H5N1 infection. The vaccinated cows developed significantly less mammary fibrosis in inoculated quarters compared to unvaccinated cows. Although we were unable to confirm a prior history of mastitis for the cows used in this study, mild fibrotic changes to the mammary gland of dairy cattle are not unexpected nor do they severely affect milk production. Vaccinated cows showed mild mammary fibrosis that could be due to a previous mastitis episode or our H5N1 2.3.4.4b virus inoculation but this did not affect milk production as compared to the unvaccinated cows. Our work highlights that the H5 mRNA–LNP 2.3.4.4b vaccine provided protection against severe fibrosing mastitis induced by H5N1 infection that will likely protect milk yields across subsequent lactations.Previous experimental challenge studies reported that the 2.3.4.4b H5N1 genotype B3.13 virus did not migrate to neighboring uninoculated mammary glands4,5,16. However, in our study, we found evidence that virus migrated from inoculated to uninoculated mammary quarters of unvaccinated cows following 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection. Viral RNA was detected in milk samples and mammary gland tissue, virus was isolated from milk samples and viral antigen was detected by IHC in mammary gland tissues of uninoculated quarters. Additionally, we observed mild clinical signs of mastitis in corresponding uninoculated quarters of unvaccinated cows. Although we also detected viral antigen by IHC in an uninoculated quarter of one vaccinated cow, we did not detect evidence of virus or viral RNA in milk or in any other sample type from this animal. These data suggest that vaccination prevented further spread of virus within the uninoculated quarter and, furthermore, prevented spread of virus outside of the mammary gland and draining lymph nodes. Our study reports 2.3.4.4b H5N1 genotype B3.13 virus migration between mammary quarters and we found that vaccination reduced viral migration in our studies. Additional studies should evaluate whether other H5N1 vaccine candidates prevent the migration of 2.3.4.4b H5N1 to neighboring uninoculated mammary glands.It will be important to monitor future antigenic changes in clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in cattle. Most of the serum neutralizing antibodies elicited by H5 mRNA–LNP vaccination in our study targeted antigenic sites A and B in the globular head of HA near the receptor-binding site. These sites have remained antigenically stable within clade 2.3.4.4b viruses and continued surveillance studies will be useful to identify any future changes in these sites. While we did not assess T cell-mediated immunity in the current study, we previously found that mRNA–LNP vaccination induces a potent CD8+ T cell response in calves6. Thus, our H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine is well matched to currently circulating clade 2.3.4.4.b viruses and also elicited T cell responses that may be protective if these viruses evolve to escape antibody responses in the future.In conclusion, our study demonstrates that the H5 mRNA–LNP 2.3.4.4b vaccine is safe and immunogenic in lactating dairy cows, eliciting robust antibody responses in sera and milk. Moreover, the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine reduced clinical disease, particularly milk loss, and significantly reduced virus shedding in milk and mammary gland fibrosis in vaccinated lactating cows. The H5 mRNA–LNP 2.3.4.4b vaccine in dairy cows provides an additional tool to use in combination with current control measures to limit the outbreak on farms, reduce spread between farms and alleviate the economic losses to the dairy industry.MethodsEthical complianceThe Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Pennsylvania Office of Animal Welfare and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Agricultural Research Service (ARS) National Animal Disease Center (NADC) reviewed and approved all studies.Study designEight Holstein lactating cows at 2–8 years of age (Supplementary Table 1) were split into two groups at the New Bolton Center Marshak dairy herd at the University of Pennsylvania and received either saline (unvaccinated) or 500 μg of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024 (H5N1) HA mRNA–LNP in saline vaccine (vaccinated) intramuscularly, directly into the muscle of the neck in front of the shoulder and below the nuchal ligament. The vaccine regimen consisted of two doses of the mRNA–LNP vaccine administered with a 3-week interval between doses. Dose and vaccine regimen were selected on the basis of our previous studies in calves6. The vaccine was created using standard techniques as previously described17. For unvaccinated cows, saline was used instead of an irrelevant or empty mRNA–LNP as our previous murine studies demonstrated no differences between saline and irrelevant mRNA–LNP controls28,29. Blood samples were collected at 0, 7, 21, 28, 41 and 49 days after vaccination, while milk samples were collected daily. Vaccinated cows were milked segregated away from the herd and their milk did not enter the human food supply. At 42 days after vaccination, cows were transported from the New Bolton Center at the University of Pennsylvania to the USDA ARS NADC in Ames. At 49 days after vaccination, cows were inoculated with 1 ml of 1 × 105 tissue culture infectious dose 50 (TCID50) per ml of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024 (H5N1) through the intramammary route in each of two quarters, using a teat canula4. The inoculation occurred after milking and standard teat disinfection and the teats were additionally disinfected with an alcohol wipe immediately before the procedure. After infusion, the inoculum was manually moved upward into the teat sinus with gentle massage.Antemortem samples such as nasal swab, ocular swab, urine, saliva, blood serum (BD vacutainer SST) and blood in EDTA (BD EDTA K2) were collected from 0 to 7 days after inoculation. Milk samples from each quarter were collected daily up to 14 days after inoculation. After milking, each cow’s bucket of milk was weighed daily from −6 to 14 days after inoculation to evaluate milk production. Lactating cows were monitored continuously for rumination using an ear-tag accelerometer sensor from −6 to 14 days after inoculation (Cow Manager SensOor, Agis Automatisering). Milk production and rumination were expressed as the percentage change relative to the pre-inoculation average. Cows were recorded daily for rectal temperature and visually monitored for clinical signs, including cough, nasal and ocular discharge and fecal consistency. Milk samples were collected by quarter and evaluated for mastitis by the CMT (ImmuCell), for consistency and for color using a visual scorecard on a scale of 0–12 (ref. 4). Samples were also collected from the bucket following milking. At 14 days after inoculation, cows were sedated using an α2-adrenergic receptor antagonist, xylazine (Rompun, Dechra), at 0.1 mg kg−1, administered i.m. Animals were then anesthetized using ketamine (Zetamine, VetOne), at 2 mg kg−1 administered intravenously (i.v.), and humanely killed by i.v. pentobarbital (Fatal-Plus, Vortech) administration per manufacturer’s dosage recommendation. At necropsy, mammary tissue from each quarter, supramammary lymph nodes and the diaphragm were collected for pathologic evaluation and virus detection by PCR as described below. The study was carried out in a working dairy farm facility at the University of Pennsylvania during the vaccination stage and in an Agricultural Biosafety level 3 (BSL3-Ag) facility at the USDA during the challenge stage. The Marshak dairy at the University of Pennsylvania was enrolled in the Pennsylvania Lactating Dairy Cattle Health Monitoring Program, which is the state’s voluntary PCR-based surveillance program that tests for H5N1 infections in dairy cattle. Weekly bulk milk tank testing was implemented before and during the study period and all samples were negative.Vaccine mRNA undetected in milkAfter prime and boost immunizations, milk samples were collected and tested for the presence of residual H5 mRNA from the vaccine. The RT–qPCR assay was performed in a QuantStudio 3 real-time PCR instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the TaqMan fast virus one-step master mix for qPCR (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacturer’s instructions and the primers/probe designed with the PrimerQuest Tool (Integrated DNA Technologies). The position and sequence of primers and probe used for the assay are reported in Supplementary Table 5. A standard curve was generated by spiking a milk sample with a known concentration of the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine. A tenfold serial dilution curve, ranging from 8 × 10−0.1 to 1010.9 mRNA copies per μl of template, was used to correlate Ct values with the amount of mRNA in milk. The limit of detection of the assay was assessed as 8 × 100.9 mRNA copies per μl of template (65 mRNA copies per μl). HA expression plasmids were cotransfected with a plasmid encoding cell surface expressed A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 neuraminidase (NA) into Expi293F cells (Thermo Fisher) with PEI Max reagent (Polysciences), following the manufacturer’s instructions. NA cleaves sialic acid and facilitates the release of the rHA into the supernatant, increasing protein yields. After 4 days, the supernatant was clarified by centrifugation. Plates were washed three times with 1× PBS + 0.1% Tween-20 and then blocked for 1 h at room temperature using blocking buffer (1× TBS, 0.05% Tween-20 and 1% BSA). Bovine serum samples were heat-inactivated at 56 °C for 1 h and then serially diluted fourfold in dilution buffer (1× TBS, 0.05% Tween-20 and 0.1% BSA). Bovine milk samples were serially diluted twofold in dilution buffer (1× TBS, 0.05% Tween-20, and 0.1% BSA). After blocking, plates were washed three times with 1× PBS + 0.1% Tween-20. Diluted milk samples were then transferred to ELISA plates and incubated for 2 h at room temperature. Importantly, these pseudoviruses can only undergo a single round of cell entry and are, therefore, not fully infectious pathogens capable of causing disease, thereby providing a safe way to study the impacts of substitutions in HA. To identify substitutions that affect neutralization by the cattle sera, deep mutational scanning libraries were incubated with serum concentrations that were sufficient to neutralize between 50% and 90% of the pseudovirus libraries, as estimated by neutralization standard used in deep mutational scanning experiments. For macroscopic evaluation, each quarter was dissected into cranial, middle and caudal sections that were assigned a percentage of fibrosis score (percent of section that was fibrotic), which was then averaged by quarter. From each cranial, middle and caudal section, three representative histologic sections were taken for a total of nine histologic sections per quarter and 36 sections per cow. Formalin-fixed tissues were transferred to 70% ethanol 48 h after collection and processed routinely for microscopic evaluation. Tissues were stained by hematoxylin and eosin stain and Picrosirius red stain per manufacturer’s instructions (AbCam) to highlight fibrosis34. Each section (36 per cow) was scored using a dual-component (intralobular and interlobular fibrosis) histologic scoring rubric that was developed to assess mammary fibrosis. Each component was independently scored on the basis of two criteria: histologic features (scale 0–4) and the percentage of tissue affected (scale 0–4). These scores were summed to produce a component-specific score ranging from 0 to 8. The overall fibrosis score was the combined total of both components (intralobular and interlobular fibrosis), yielding a maximum possible score of 16. The results by quarter were summed for a possible total of 144 and then the median by status (uninoculated or inoculated) of gland within a cow (Supplementary Tables 6 and 7). The percent changes in rumination, milk production and milk PCR in the uninoculated quarters were analyzed with a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by a Tukey’s multiple-comparison test to compare vaccinated versus unvaccinated groups across days after inoculation. Viral RNA detection by RT–qPCR in the inoculated quarters were analyzed by a mixed-effects model (residual maximum likelihood model) followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Differences in mammary microscopic lesions (fibrosis) and mammary macroscopic lesions between vaccinated and unvaccinated cows were evaluated using the Mann–Whitney U-test. Statistical significance was evaluated using an α threshold of 0.05. P values greater than 0.05 were considered not significant. Pearson’s correlation coefficients in unvaccinated and vaccinated lactating cows were calculated between Ct values (milk bucket and milk from inoculated and uninoculated quarters) and parameters: milk production (n = 56), rumination time (n = 58), CMT scores from inoculated quarters (n = 60) and uninoculated quarters (n = 60), milk color from inoculated quarters (n = 60) and uninoculated quarters (n = 60) and milk consistency scores from inoculated quarters (n = 60) and uninoculated quarters (n = 60), across all time points, using GraphPad Prism Software version 10 (GraphPad Software).
